subtopic_detail: Breast lump in a lactating woman that has not resolved with appropriate treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old woman who is nine weeks postpartum and breastfeeding. Three weeks ago you treated her for a hot tender left breast with a full course of flucloxacillin, and the fever and redness settled within four days.

The lump itself has not gone. She says it feels the same size or slightly larger, and the skin over it has become dimpled and thickened in the last week. She is afebrile and systemically well and milk supply is good. On examination there is a firm irregular 4 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, tethered to overlying skin with peau d'orange, and a 1.5 cm firm mobile node in the left axilla. The breast is not warm and there is no fluctuance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 116/70, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular 4 cm mass in the left upper outer quadrant tethered to skin with peau d'orange, no fluctuance or warmth, 1.5 cm firm mobile left axillary node
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe a second longer course of flucloxacillin and review in two weeks
options.rationale: A further antibiotic course is justified when infection is still active with fever, warmth and raised inflammatory markers, and none of those persist here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Advise her to wean from the left breast and review the lump afterwards
options.rationale: Stopping feeding causes engorgement and stasis, and it neither treats infection nor advances the assessment of a persistent mass (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association; Cancer Australia Breast Changes).

options.text: Refer for incision and drainage of the collection under local anaesthetic
options.rationale: Drainage treats an abscess, which is fluctuant and tender with a collection on imaging, and current practice favours ultrasound guided aspiration over open incision in any case (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Reassure that this is a blocked duct and teach positioning and massage
options.rationale: A blocked duct is a soft tender segmental swelling that changes with a feed, not a hard mass tethering the skin with an axillary node (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Arrange urgent breast imaging with biopsy and continue breastfeeding
options.rationale: A lump that persists after adequate treatment of infection, with skin tethering and a node, requires triple assessment on an urgent pathway, and lactation is not a reason to delay imaging or core biopsy (Source: Cancer Australia Breast Changes).

explanation.summary: Breast cancer occurring in pregnancy or lactation is uncommon but is diagnosed late with depressing regularity, because the symptoms are attributed to mastitis and treated with successive antibiotic courses. The safeguard is a fixed rule rather than clinical impression: any mass that does not fully resolve after appropriate treatment of infection gets imaged. Ultrasound is the first modality in a lactating breast, with mammography added as needed, and core biopsy is safe during lactation with a small risk of a milk fistula. Peau d'orange with a rapidly enlarging breast raises inflammatory carcinoma, which is frequently mistaken for infection and carries a worse prognosis when the diagnosis is delayed.
key_points: Any breast lump persisting after treated mastitis requires imaging
Ultrasound is the first line modality in a lactating breast
Core biopsy is safe during lactation and should not be deferred
Skin tethering, peau d'orange and a firm node are not features of infection
Weaning does not need to precede assessment
explanation.pearls: Mastitis that fails to resolve within two weeks of appropriate antibiotics is imaged rather than re-treated, because inflammatory carcinoma is the diagnosis most often lost to a second antibiotic course.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing antibiotics and evacuation in secondary postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar called to the emergency department. A 29 year old woman is 12 days after a normal vaginal birth at term with an estimated blood loss of 350 mL at delivery. Her lochia had almost stopped, but for two days she has been soaking a pad every hour and passing clots.

She has lower abdominal pain and offensive vaginal discharge. She is not dizzy and has passed urine normally. On examination the uterus is bulky and tender at the level of the umbilicus, the os admits a fingertip, and there is no cervical or vaginal laceration. Bedside ultrasound shows heterogeneous echogenic material of 22 mm within the cavity with vascularity on colour Doppler. Bleeding continues while you examine her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112, blood pressure 104/62, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.3
data_table.Examination: Bulky tender uterus at the umbilicus, offensive lochia, os admits a fingertip, no genital tract laceration
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165); white cell count 18.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); ultrasound shows 22 mm of vascular echogenic intracavity material

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous antibiotics and evacuate the uterus once cover is running
options.rationale: Bleeding this heavy with retained vascular tissue will not settle on antibiotics alone, and instrumenting an infected uterus before antibiotics are circulating provokes bacteraemia, so cover is started first and the evacuation follows promptly by an experienced operator (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Take her directly to theatre for curettage before antibiotics are started
options.rationale: Curettage of an infected soft puerperal uterus without antibiotic cover risks bacteraemia and perforation, and the few minutes taken to start the infusion do not delay haemostasis meaningfully (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage).

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review her in the clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: Oral therapy with outpatient review suits a woman who is haemodynamically stable with light bleeding, and a pulse of 112 with a haemoglobin of 92 g/L is not that patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give intramuscular ergometrine and observe her on the ward overnight
options.rationale: Uterotonics reduce bleeding from an atonic uterus but cannot expel adherent vascular tissue, and observation alone leaves both the haemorrhage and the sepsis untreated (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage).

options.text: Arrange uterine artery embolisation as the initial definitive intervention
options.rationale: Embolisation is the option for bleeding that continues after evacuation or for a suspected arteriovenous malformation, not the first line for retained products with endometritis (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum Haemorrhage).

explanation.summary: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks after birth and is usually caused by retained products, endometritis, or both together, since retained tissue is the substrate that infection grows in. The clinical judgement is about sequence rather than about which single treatment to pick. Antibiotics are started first so that the operator is not disseminating organisms during instrumentation, and evacuation follows without a prolonged delay when bleeding is heavy. Curettage of the soft postpartum uterus carries a real risk of perforation and of later intrauterine adhesions, so it is done gently, ideally under ultrasound guidance and by a senior operator. Persistent bleeding after evacuation should prompt thought about an arteriovenous malformation or gestational trophoblastic disease.
key_points: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage spans 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth
Retained products and endometritis usually coexist
Start antibiotics before instrumenting an infected uterus
Gentle evacuation by a senior operator limits perforation and adhesion risk
Consider arteriovenous malformation or trophoblastic disease if bleeding persists
explanation.pearls: Send the evacuated tissue for histology in every secondary postpartum haemorrhage, because gestational trophoblastic disease presents this way and a normal beta human chorionic gonadotropin at the time does not exclude it.

subtopic_detail: Entry dyspareunia with normal vulval skin and repeatedly negative swabs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman with 12 months of burning pain at the vaginal opening that starts as soon as penetration is attempted and lasts for hours afterwards. She has no pain at other times and no pain with tampons at first, although she now avoids them too.

She has taken four courses of oral fluconazole prescribed for presumed thrush over the past year, each with no benefit. She is in a stable relationship, describes the relationship as supportive, and has no history of sexual assault. On examination the vulval skin is normal in colour and architecture with no fissures, whitening or loss of the labia minora. A cotton bud applied to the vestibule reproduces her pain sharply at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions but not on the labia majora or perineum, and the pelvic floor is tight with tenderness of the levator muscles.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval skin colour and architecture, allodynia localised to the vestibule at 5 and 7 o'clock on cotton bud testing, hypertonic tender levator ani
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab no candida or bacterial vaginosis; nucleic acid testing negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea; vaginal pH 4.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a six month course of weekly oral fluconazole for recurrent thrush
options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy is for culture proven recurrent candidiasis, and repeatedly negative swabs with no response to four courses make that diagnosis untenable (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

options.text: Apply topical clobetasol propionate ointment nightly for four weeks
options.rationale: Potent topical corticosteroid is the treatment for an inflammatory dermatosis such as lichen sclerosus, whose defining features are whitening and architectural change that are absent here (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

options.text: Refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy and start topical local anaesthetic
options.rationale: Localised provoked vestibular pain with pelvic floor hypertonicity responds to muscle directed physiotherapy combined with topical anaesthetic and vulval care, which together form the accepted first line (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders; International Society for the Study of Vulvovaginal Disease).
source_refs: International Society for the Study of Vulvovaginal Disease

options.text: Refer for surgical vestibulectomy on the next elective operating list
options.rationale: Vestibulectomy is considered only after a documented failure of conservative treatment over months, because operating on an untreated hypertonic pelvic floor gives poor results (Source: International Society for the Study of Vulvovaginal Disease).
source_refs: International Society for the Study of Vulvovaginal Disease

options.text: Change her combined oral contraceptive to a progestogen only preparation
options.rationale: An association between early combined contraceptive use and vestibulodynia is debated and switching alone does not treat established pain (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Disorders).

explanation.summary: Provoked vestibulodynia is the commonest cause of entry dyspareunia in younger women and is a pain condition rather than an infection or a dermatosis. The diagnosis is made on the cotton bud test, which maps allodynia to the vestibule while the surrounding vulval skin remains normal, and by the absence of positive microbiology. Most women arrive after repeated empirical antifungal courses, and the repeated failure of those courses is itself diagnostic information. Treatment is multimodal, combining pelvic floor physiotherapy for the secondary muscle hypertonicity, topical anaesthetic, vulval care advice and psychological support, with tricyclics or gabapentinoids added for persistent pain and surgery kept as a last resort.
key_points: The cotton bud test localises the allodynia and makes the diagnosis
Normal vulval architecture excludes lichen sclerosus
Negative swabs after repeated antifungal failure argue against candidiasis
Pelvic floor hypertonicity is a secondary driver and needs physiotherapy
Vestibulectomy follows failure of conservative treatment, not precedes it
explanation.pearls: Four failed courses of fluconazole in a woman with negative swabs should stop the antifungal cycle and start the cotton bud test, because pain reproduced only at the vestibule points to a neuropathic and muscular problem rather than to infection.

sources.label: International Society for the Study of Vulvovaginal Disease

subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception choice when body weight reduces oral efficacy
stem:
You are the doctor in a community sexual health clinic. A 26 year old woman attends 68 hours after a condom broke. Her cycles are regular at 28 days and today is day 13.

She weighs 104 kg with a body mass index of 38 kg per square metre. She is not using any regular contraception, has never been pregnant, and has no contraindication to any method. She has taken no medication in the past month. She says she does not want to be pregnant under any circumstances, and separately she would like to start something reliable and long lasting today so that she is not back here again. A urine pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg per square metre, abdomen soft and non tender, no cervical excitation or adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative; nucleic acid testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea taken today

options.text: Give levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally now and start a progestogen only pill
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel efficacy falls with increasing body weight and is markedly reduced above about 70 kg, and it is also the least effective option this late after intercourse (Source: Family Planning Australia Emergency Contraception).

options.text: Insert a copper intrauterine device today and screen for infection
options.rationale: The copper device is the most effective emergency method with a failure rate under 1 per cent, its action is not reduced by body weight or by the delay to 68 hours, and it converts the visit into ongoing long acting contraception (Source: Family Planning Australia Emergency Contraception; RANZCOG Long Acting Reversible Contraception).

options.text: Give levonorgestrel 3 mg orally now as a double dose for her weight
options.rationale: Doubling the dose is sometimes offered when no better option exists, but the evidence that it restores efficacy is weak and it should not displace a method that works (Source: Family Planning Australia Emergency Contraception).

options.text: Give ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally and start a pill tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Ulipristal outperforms levonorgestrel near ovulation but its efficacy also falls at higher body weight, and starting a progestogen within five days blunts its action (Source: Family Planning Australia Emergency Contraception).

options.text: Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device today as emergency cover
options.rationale: The hormonal device is excellent ongoing contraception, but it is the copper ion rather than the progestogen that provides the emergency effect, so it is the near pair that fails the immediate task (Source: RANZCOG Long Acting Reversible Contraception).

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception decisions turn on three variables: time since intercourse, position in the cycle, and body weight. Oral methods act by delaying ovulation, so they fail if the luteinising hormone surge has already begun, and day 13 of a 28 day cycle is precisely the highest risk window. The copper intrauterine device works after fertilisation as well as before, which is why it retains its efficacy up to five days after intercourse or five days after the earliest estimated ovulation. Both oral agents lose efficacy at higher body weight, and the woman who also wants ongoing contraception gains twice from the device. Screening swabs are taken at insertion rather than waiting for results, since delaying insertion is the greater risk.
key_points: Copper device failure rate is under 1 per cent and is unaffected by body weight
Oral emergency contraception works by delaying ovulation and fails after the surge
Levonorgestrel efficacy falls above about 70 kg
Ulipristal is blunted by starting a progestogen within five days
The hormonal intrauterine device is not an emergency contraceptive
explanation.pearls: A copper intrauterine device can be inserted up to five days after the earliest estimated ovulation rather than five days after intercourse, which extends the window well past day five in a woman who presents late in her cycle.

subtopic_detail: Cyclical mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase and the evidence needed before treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman who describes becoming a different person for about a week each month. She is irritable to the point of shouting at her children, tearful, bloated and exhausted, and has twice taken sick leave because she could not face work.

She says the symptoms lift within a day or two of her period starting and that she feels entirely well for the following fortnight. This has happened for at least six months. She has no history of mental illness, drinks two standard drinks a week, and is not using hormonal contraception. Her thyroid function and full blood count taken last month were normal, and today, on day 8 of her cycle, her mental state examination is entirely unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination normal today with euthymic mood, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-165); ferritin 46 mcg/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily continuously and review her in four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonergic antidepressant is effective for this condition and can be given continuously or in the luteal phase only, but treatment follows confirmation rather than preceding it (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without a break
options.rationale: Continuous combined contraception is a reasonable second line treatment, and prescribing it now removes the cyclical pattern that the diagnosis depends on demonstrating (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

options.text: Refer to psychiatry for assessment of possible bipolar II disorder now
options.rationale: Bipolar II requires discrete hypomanic episodes of at least four days with elevated or expansive mood and increased activity, and irritability tied to the luteal phase is not that (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

options.text: Ask her to complete daily symptom ratings over two menstrual cycles
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings across at least two cycles showing symptoms in the final week before menses that improve within days of onset and are absent in the follicular phase, because retrospective report agrees poorly with prospective data (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders; DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Advise calcium and vitamin B6 supplements and review her in three months
options.rationale: Supplements have modest evidence for physical premenstrual symptoms, and offering them as the whole plan understates the functional impairment she describes (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is distinguished from premenstrual syndrome by the severity of the mood symptoms and the functional impairment they cause, and it is distinguished from an underlying mood disorder by the symptom free follicular phase. Around half of women who report a premenstrual pattern retrospectively do not confirm it on prospective daily ratings, and many instead have premenstrual exacerbation of an existing depressive or anxiety disorder, which needs different treatment. Two cycles of prospective ratings therefore change management in a substantial minority of cases. Once confirmed, serotonergic antidepressants work rapidly enough to be given only in the luteal phase, which distinguishes this condition from major depression where continuous treatment is required.
key_points: Prospective daily ratings across two cycles are required for the diagnosis
A symptom free follicular phase separates it from premenstrual exacerbation
Retrospective report agrees poorly with prospective data
Serotonergic antidepressants can be dosed in the luteal phase only
Continuous combined contraception is a reasonable second line option
explanation.pearls: Serotonergic antidepressants relieve premenstrual dysphoric symptoms within a day or two rather than the two to four weeks needed in major depression, which is why luteal phase only dosing from ovulation to menses is a legitimate regimen.
